cards.prompt: Sort df by revenue, lowest to highest.
cards.why: sort_values() reorders rows by the values in a column; ascending order is the default.
cards.whenToUse: Ranking rows by a numeric or string column.
cards.commonMistake: Forgetting the column name is a string, e.g. writing df.sort_values(revenue).
cards.example:
#   region category  revenue  units
# 4   West     Bags       45      5
# 6  North    Shoes       50      5
# ...
# 0   West    Shoes      120     12

cards.prompt: Sort df by revenue, highest to lowest.
cards.why: ascending=False reverses the default sort order.
cards.whenToUse: Ranking rows from biggest to smallest.
cards.commonMistake: Sorting ascending then calling .iloc[::-1] instead of just passing ascending=False.
cards.example:
#   region category  revenue  units
# 0   West    Shoes      120     12
# 1   East    Shoes       95      9
# ...
# 4   West     Bags       45      5

cards.prompt: Sort df by region first, then by revenue within each region, both ascending.
cards.why: Passing a list of columns sorts by the first column, using later columns only to break ties.
cards.whenToUse: A primary sort key with a secondary tiebreaker.
cards.commonMistake: Sorting by revenue alone and losing the grouping by region.
cards.example:
#   region category  revenue  units
# 3   East     Bags       60      6
# 5   East    Shoes       70      7
# 1   East    Shoes       95      9
# 6  North    Shoes       50      5
# ...

cards.prompt: Sort df by region ascending, but by revenue descending within each region.
cards.why: Passing a list to ascending lets each sort key have its own direction.
cards.whenToUse: Multi-column sorts where the columns need different directions.
cards.commonMistake: Passing a single ascending=False, which reverses every key instead of just one.
cards.example:
#   region category  revenue  units
# 1   East    Shoes       95      9
# 5   East    Shoes       70      7
# 3   East     Bags       60      6
# ...

cards.prompt: You have df.iloc[[5, 2, 7]], rows out of their original order. Restore the original row order using the index.
cards.why: sort_index() sorts by the row labels rather than any column's values, restoring the original order if labels weren't changed.
cards.whenToUse: Undoing a reorder that came from filtering, sampling, or a previous sort_values() call.
cards.commonMistake: Calling sort_values() instead, which sorts by data, not by the index labels.
cards.example:
#   region category  revenue  units
# 2   West     Bags       80      8
# 5   East    Shoes       70      7
# 7  North     Bags       65      6

cards.prompt: Sort df's columns alphabetically, left to right.
cards.why: sort_index(axis=1) sorts the column labels instead of the row labels.
cards.whenToUse: Getting a consistent, predictable column order regardless of how the DataFrame was built.
cards.commonMistake: Forgetting axis=1 — the default axis=0 sorts rows, not columns.
cards.example:
#   category  region  revenue  units
# 0    Shoes    West      120     12

cards.prompt: Get the 3 rows with the highest revenue.
cards.why: nlargest() sorts and slices in a single call, clearer than sort_values().head().
cards.whenToUse: You only need the top N rows, not the full ranking.
cards.commonMistake: Writing sort_values('revenue', ascending=False).head(3) when nlargest(3, 'revenue') says the same thing more directly.
cards.example:
#   region category  revenue  units
# 0   West    Shoes      120     12
# 1   East    Shoes       95      9
# 2   West     Bags       80      8

cards.prompt: Get the 2 rows with the lowest revenue.
cards.why: nsmallest() is the mirror of nlargest() — smallest values instead of largest.
cards.whenToUse: You need the bottom N rows by some metric, e.g. worst performers.
cards.commonMistake: Using nlargest() with a negative count instead of switching to nsmallest().
cards.example:
#   region category  revenue  units
# 4   West     Bags       45      5
# 6  North    Shoes       50      5

cards.prompt: Give every row a rank by revenue, where rank 1 is the highest revenue.
cards.why: rank() assigns a position to every value instead of reordering the rows themselves.
cards.whenToUse: You need each row's standing (1st, 2nd, 3rd...) without changing row order.
cards.commonMistake: Assuming rank() sorts the DataFrame — it only adds rank numbers, the row order is unchanged.

cards.prompt: Sort df by region, then by category, both ascending — a simple two-key sort with no mixed directions.
cards.why: When every key sorts the same direction, a plain list of column names is enough — no need for the ascending= list.
cards.whenToUse: Multi-key sorts where all keys share the same direction.
cards.commonMistake: Reaching for ascending=[True, True] when the plain default already does that.
cards.example:
#   region category  revenue  units
# 3   East     Bags       60      6
# 1   East    Shoes       95      9
# 5   East    Shoes       70      7
# ...

cards.prompt: Sort df by revenue, highest first. Fill in the blank.
cards.why: ascending=False reverses sort_values()'s default low-to-high order.
cards.whenToUse: Ranking rows from biggest to smallest.
cards.commonMistake: Passing ascending=0 or ascending='False' (a string) instead of the boolean False.
cards.example:
#   region category  revenue  units
# 0   West    Shoes      120     12
# 1   East    Shoes       95      9

cards.prompt: Get the top 3 rows by revenue using sort_values and head instead of nlargest.
cards.why: sort_values().head(n) is the more explicit two-step equivalent of nlargest(n, col).
cards.whenToUse: When you want the sorted order visible in code, not just the top slice.
cards.commonMistake: Forgetting ascending=False and getting the bottom 3 rows instead of the top 3.
cards.example:
#   region category  revenue  units
# 0   West    Shoes      120     12
# 1   East    Shoes       95      9
# 2   West     Bags       80      8

cards.prompt: Total units sold per category, sorted lowest to highest.
cards.why: Chaining sort_values() after a groupby aggregation ranks the resulting groups by their summary value.
cards.whenToUse: Ranking aggregated groups rather than raw rows.
cards.commonMistake: Calling sort_values() before groupby(), which sorts the raw rows and has no effect on the aggregated order.

cards.prompt: Sort df by revenue descending, and give the result a fresh 0..n index directly in the same call.
cards.why: ignore_index=True discards the old row labels and assigns a new 0..n-1 range, without a separate reset_index() call.
cards.whenToUse: Sorting when the original index values are meaningless afterward anyway.
cards.commonMistake: Forgetting ignore_index=True and ending up with a shuffled, non-sequential index.
cards.example:
#   region category  revenue  units
# 0   West    Shoes      120     12
# 1   East    Shoes       95      9

cards.prompt: Which call correctly returns the single row (as a Series) with the highest revenue?
cards.why: idxmax() finds the index label of the maximum value, and loc[...] on a single label returns a Series (one row).
cards.whenToUse: Grabbing one specific row identified by an extreme value in some column.
cards.commonMistake: Using nlargest(1, 'revenue'), which returns a one-row DataFrame, not a Series — a different shape than 'the row'.
cards.example:
# region     West
# category  Shoes
# revenue     120
# units       12
